packs.title: Heritage and Lakes
packs.promise: Explore Hanoi through scholarly courtyards, museum evidence, public facades and two different lakes.

q.s: Turn one gallery observation into an original arrangement.
st: During the paid gallery visit, choose one currently displayed work that you can comfortably see. Remember its label and one compositional decision: a large shape, an empty area, a repeated edge or an off-centre subject.

After leaving the galleries, make your own small arrangement on paper or in a phone note. Use three simple shapes or three short lines of description to apply that decision to something from your own day; do not reproduce the whole artwork.
Give your arrangement a title and explain what you borrowed from the work’s layout. Keep the artist/title as actually read separate from your own invented subject.

q.s: Compare a standing monument with evidence beneath it.
st: Follow the current visitor circuit to an open ground-level view of Doan Mon. Collect one visible architectural detail and one fact from its actual interpretation.
Find a currently admitted archaeological display or panel elsewhere on the circuit. Collect a material or structural trace and the period or context actually supplied by its label.

Arrange those two witnesses in a small earlier/later comparison using their labels. Explain what a standing structure lets you see that a fragment does not, and what the fragment might reveal that the standing structure cannot. Mark any uncertainty rather than guessing dates.

q.s: Pause beside West Lake without adding another destination.
st: Find a comfortable currently open public-pavement position, back from the water and clear of the walking route. Sit only if an open public seat is available and suitable.
Spend a few unhurried minutes with the West Lake view. Choose one steady visual detail and one changing sound or movement, without recording people or trying to identify every landmark.
After the pause, write a short account of those two details and how your attention changed. The account can be plain observations; no spiritual practice or temple visit is part of it.

packs.title: Old Quarter Work and Memory
packs.promise: Explore a connected Old Quarter area through household space, craft, goods, painted memory and public garden time.

q.s: Collect how a guild house is put together.
st: After lawful entry, collect a visible support, a joining detail and a decoration from the currently admitted architectural view. Choose details you can see without touching or entering a worship-only area.

For each detail, describe its visible material or shape and what job you think it does. Use a visitor label if available, and mark your own structural or decorative interpretation as a possibility rather than a documented guild technique.

Arrange your three details as a short building-making sequence: what holds, what connects and what gives character. Link it to the actual craft-guild house you visited, without claiming that an absent workshop or display was available.

q.s: Read how goods are arranged to move through a market.
st: Choose two visible goods displays from the public street—bundles, stacks, baskets or packages that can be observed without entering a stall. Keep vendors and customers out of your record unless they consent.
For each, collect a clue about storage or handling: how items repeat, are grouped, are protected, or can be moved. Describe the actual arrangement before interpreting what it might make easier.

Compare the two arrangements in a short goods-to-street account. Explain which visible detail suggests handling several items together, and which detail still leaves the quantity or sale method uncertain. No purchase or price survey is needed.

q.s: Answer a public mural with an original everyday scene.
st: Choose one currently visible mural panel from lawful public sidewalk. Identify an actual everyday action or setting depicted in it without copying lettering or claiming you recognize every historical person.

Notice one real feature in today’s surrounding street that differs from the painted scene. Step to a clear public place and create a short original continuation: a three-line scene, a small sketch, or a spoken scene you transcribe afterward.

Give your continuation one new everyday action inspired by that real present-day detail. Explain which part came from the mural, which from your street observation, and which you invented. Keep it separate from a claim about the original artist’s intention.
